title: Elastic Beanstalk Adds Cluster Mode, Running Applications on Shared EKS Clusters
gist: AWS added a new EKS-backed 'Cluster Mode' to Elastic Beanstalk for running containerized app portfolios on shared, service-managed Kubernetes clusters, but the launch messaging overstates deployment flexibility and lock-in mitigation relative to what the documentation actually specifies, and the pricing model adds cluster and management fees that undercut the promised cost savings at smaller scale.

insights.claim: AWS added Cluster Mode to Elastic Beanstalk, which runs applications as containers on Amazon EKS clusters that the service creates and operates, sitting alongside the existing EC2-based environment type now renamed Beanstalk Standard.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Signals AWS continuing to fold Kubernetes-based execution into its higher-level PaaS products, widening the abstraction layers competing for the same workloads (Beanstalk, ECS, EKS Auto Mode, Lambda).
insights.locator: AWS recently added Cluster Mode to Elastic Beanstalk

insights.claim: Customers cannot choose which EKS cluster their Elastic Beanstalk Cluster Mode environment lands on or its Kubernetes version; environments in the same account sharing the same VPC subnet set share a cluster, a different subnet set gets a different cluster created on first use in about ten minutes, and existing subnets/cluster IAM roles cannot be changed without recreating the environment.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The subnet set is a one-time, unchangeable decision that determines cost-sharing, isolation, and infrastructure control, so adopting teams must architect subnet strategy correctly before first deployment.
insights.locator: Customers do not pick the cluster

insights.claim: Direct access to the underlying EKS cluster is not offered; infrastructure access is service-managed only through the Elastic Beanstalk API, AWS CLI, or console, and if the cluster is changed outside Elastic Beanstalk, the service detects configuration drift, stops maintaining the cluster, places no new environments on it, and fails updates until the drift is reverted.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: This is a materially higher lock-in and lower-control model than raw EKS; teams needing direct cluster control or custom operators should avoid Cluster Mode.
insights.locator: Direct access to the cluster is not part of the model either

insights.claim: AWS's launch messaging claims Cluster Mode supports immutable and traffic-splitting deployments as benefits, but the architecture documentation only shows rolling update (the default) or all-at-once deployment options, and the What's New post lists neither immutable nor traffic-splitting; immutable deployments remain exclusive to Beanstalk Standard.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A concrete example of marketing-documentation mismatch at AWS; investors/practitioners evaluating AWS service claims should verify against developer-guide-level docs rather than launch blog posts.
insights.locator: Deployment options are also narrower than the launch blog suggests

insights.claim: Network traffic between environments on a shared Cluster Mode cluster is blocked by default with no option to disable the blocking, but AWS's own guide still recommends separate subnet sets (and thus separate clusters) for environments serving different end customers, running code the customer doesn't control, or under compliance regimes requiring infrastructure separation, explicitly stating shared-cluster controls do not make it equivalent to separate clusters.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Regulated or multi-tenant SaaS customers cannot rely on Cluster Mode's default isolation alone and must pay for separate clusters, eroding the cost-saving pitch for exactly the customers most likely to need compliance guarantees (HIPAA, PCI DSS, SOC, FedRAMP, IRAP are cited as in-scope programs).
insights.quote: The controls described in the rest of this topic separate environments on a shared cluster, but they do not make a shared cluster equivalent to separate clusters.
insights.locator: On isolation, network traffic between environments

insights.claim: Elastic Beanstalk Cluster Mode has no platform fee and bills compute at EC2 rates, but adds a flat hourly EKS fee per cluster and an EKS Auto Mode management fee on top of instance costs that EC2 discounts like Savings Plans or Spot cannot reduce; each load-balanced environment also gets its own Application Load Balancer and pod-level metrics are metered per resource, making monitoring potentially costlier than Standard.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Cost savings only materialize through shared-node density across many applications; teams running few applications or small portfolios should expect Cluster Mode to cost more than Standard, per AWS's own guidance.
insights.locator: The economics depend on the same sharing

insights.claim: AWS's own overview describes Beanstalk Standard (the EC2-based mode) as the cost-effective choice for smaller or fewer applications and as the only mode supporting Windows.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: AWS itself is segmenting the two products by portfolio size, implicitly conceding Cluster Mode is not a universal upgrade over Standard.

insights.claim: Paul Pollack, an AWS software engineering manager, addressed vendor lock-in concerns in the launch post by stating customers can take over management of their application's resources if needed with Cluster Mode.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: AWS is proactively countering the lock-in narrative, suggesting it anticipates this as a key adoption objection from enterprise architects.
insights.quote: With Cluster Mode you can take over management of your application's resources if you ever need to.
insights.locator: Paul Pollack, a software engineering manager at AWS

insights.claim: James Eastham of Datadog publicly questioned where Cluster Mode fits relative to EKS, EKS Auto Mode, ECS, ECS Express Mode, classic Beanstalk, Lambda containers and Lambda Managed Instances, comparing the overlap to 'SNS vs EventBridge all over again,' and after AWS's response still maintained that 'ECS and Beanstalk Cluster mode seem a little close to each other when they could actually just put a bunch of effort into making one of the services great.'
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Highlights AWS's persistent internal product-overlap/fragmentation problem across its compute portfolio, a recurring criticism from experienced AWS architects that can slow enterprise adoption decisions and increase evaluation cost for customers.
insights.quote: This feels like SNS vs EventBridge all over again
insights.locator: The launch also raised the question of where Cluster Mode fits

insights.claim: Cluster Mode is available in all commercial AWS Regions where Elastic Beanstalk operates, is not eligible for the AWS Free Tier, and can be deployed via console, AWS CLI, EB CLI, CloudFormation, Terraform, a new GitHub Action, and agent skills.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Broad immediate regional availability plus IaC tooling support signals AWS is treating this as a general-availability product push rather than a limited preview.
insights.locator: Cluster Mode is available in all commercial AWS Regions

insights.claim: Applications on Cluster Mode must fit a stateless model with interchangeable replicas and ephemeral local storage, and when subnets are omitted, environments land in the public subnets of the default VPC.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Stateful legacy applications are not candidates for migration to Cluster Mode; default-subnet behavior is a security footgun for teams that don't explicitly configure subnets.
